questions.sub_skill: Configure and deploy AI Gateway in Azure API Management for Microsoft Foundry
questions.prompt: One application's runaway loop starves every other consumer of your Foundry deployment. Token metrics show a single consumer at its limit. What is most likely misconfigured?
options: The token limit is set per minute rather than per day
The llm-token-limit counter key is a constant rather than the subscription, so all consumers share one counter
Semantic caching is disabled
The backend pool has no circuit breaker
questions.explanation: Limiting by a key every consumer shares reproduces the problem you were solving. A per-consumer counter key — the subscription ID — means one application hitting its limit leaves the others working.
why_not: The window size changes how quickly a consumer reaches its limit, not whether one consumer's usage starves the others.
Semantic caching reduces backend calls for repeated prompts. It does not separate one consumer's quota from another's.
A circuit breaker protects against a failing backend. The problem here is one shared token counter.
questions.scenario_clue: "one application's runaway loop starves every other consumer" - a shared token counter.
questions.misconception: That any token limit isolates consumers, whatever counter key it uses.

questions.sub_skill: Configure and deploy AI Gateway in Azure API Management for Microsoft Foundry
questions.prompt: Once a consumer has used up its token allowance, its further requests must be refused at the gateway rather than reaching the model and incurring backend cost. Which setting?
options: Semantic caching with a low similarity threshold
estimate-prompt-tokens on the llm-token-limit policy
A backend circuit breaker
An llm-emit-token-metric dimension on prompt length
questions.explanation: With estimate-prompt-tokens set to true, llm-token-limit estimates prompt tokens from the API's prompt schema before forwarding, which can stop requests reaching the backend once the limit is already exceeded. Set to false, the policy counts from the model's response, so the request that pushes a consumer over the limit has already reached the model.
why_not: Semantic caching answers repeated prompts from the cache. It does not reject oversized ones.
A circuit breaker reacts to backend failures. It does not measure prompt size.
Emitting a metric reports token usage after the fact. It rejects nothing.
questions.scenario_clue: "refused at the gateway rather than reaching the model" - the gateway must estimate prompt tokens before forwarding.
questions.misconception: That a token limit can only react after the backend has already processed the request.

questions.sub_skill: Configure guardrails for agent security in Foundry
questions.prompt: Your team sets strict harm-category thresholds in the guardrail on a Foundry model deployment. A new agent built on that deployment has its own guardrail assigned, with no controls on tool responses. The team says indirect prompt injection arriving through the agent's tools is handled. Why is it not?
options: Harm-category controls only scan completions, never prompts
Harm categories govern harmful content, not injected instructions; and the agent uses its own guardrail, which has no indirect attack control on the tool response intervention point
Agent guardrails are applied only after the model guardrail has already blocked the content
Indirect injection can only be detected at the API Management gateway
questions.explanation: Indirect attacks are a separate risk (Prompt Shields), not a harm category. And an agent with its own guardrail is governed by that guardrail alone - it fully overrides the model deployment's. Content returned by a tool is scanned only if the agent's guardrail has a control on the tool response intervention point.
why_not: Harm-category controls can scan user input and output. The gap is that injected instructions are not a harm category, and the agent's own guardrail has no tool response control.
The agent's guardrail does not run after the model's - it fully replaces it for that agent. The model deployment's thresholds no longer apply to the agent.

The gateway's llm-content-safety policy is one place to check prompts, but tool responses inside an agent's orchestration are scanned by the agent's guardrail, at the tool response intervention point.
questions.scenario_clue: "its own guardrail assigned" and "no controls on tool responses" - the agent ignores the model's guardrail, and nothing scans what tools return.
questions.misconception: That strict content filtering on the model also protects an agent built on it against injected instructions.

questions.sub_skill: Enable Defender for AI Service in Cloud Workload Protection in Defender for Cloud
questions.prompt: Defender for AI Services raises a jailbreak alert on a Foundry model deployment. The SOC asks what the prompt actually said. Under what configuration can you show them?
options: Always - every alert includes the full prompt and response
Only if the plan's suspicious prompt evidence (user prompt evidence) component is on; otherwise the alert still fires but the prompt content is masked
Only if the data security for AI interactions component sends the prompts to Microsoft Purview
Only if API Management request logging was enabled in front of the model
questions.explanation: Suspicious prompt evidence adds redacted snippets of the suspicious parts of prompts and responses to each alert. With it off, Defender keeps analysing prompts and alerting, but the prompt content is masked in the alert.
why_not: Alerts never carry the full conversation. Even with prompt evidence on, they contain redacted snippets of the suspicious segments.
The Purview component supports classification, audit and eDiscovery in Purview. The snippet inside the Defender alert comes from the suspicious prompt evidence component.
Gateway logs are a separate record you would have to build. The question is what the Defender alert itself can show, which depends on suspicious prompt evidence.
questions.scenario_clue: "what the prompt actually said" inside a Defender alert points to suspicious prompt evidence.
questions.misconception: That a detection alert automatically includes the evidence an investigator needs.

questions.sub_skill: Monitor AI security by using the Data and AI security dashboard in Defender for Cloud
questions.prompt: A subscription has Defender CSPM enabled but has never enabled Defender for AI Services. A Foundry resource in it is targeted by repeated jailbreak attempts. What will the Data and AI security dashboard show?
options: The jailbreak attempts as alerts, because Defender CSPM includes AI threat detection
The Foundry resource under AI discovery with its posture and recommendations, but no AI threat protection alerts, because runtime detection comes from Defender for AI Services
Nothing at all - AI resources are only discovered when Defender for AI Services is on
Only the attack attempts, with no inventory, because posture needs Defender for AI Services
questions.explanation: Discovery and posture for AI resources come from Defender CSPM (AI security posture management). Runtime threat detection comes from Defender for AI Services. The dashboard reflects the plans enabled, so the resource appears but the attacks go undetected.
why_not: Defender CSPM provides discovery, recommendations and attack paths for AI resources. It does not inspect prompts at runtime.
AI discovery is part of Defender CSPM. The resource appears; what is missing is runtime threat detection.
It is the other way round: CSPM supplies the inventory and posture, and the missing plan is the one that would supply alerts.
questions.scenario_clue: "Defender CSPM enabled but ... never enabled Defender for AI Services" - posture yes, runtime detection no.
questions.misconception: That AI discovery and AI threat detection come from the same plan.
